title: Auto-Tag Every Campaign Link with UTM Parameters
summary: Stop hand-building tracking links. Write a script that tags a whole spreadsheet of URLs consistently in under a second.

certification.description: Strings: methods, slicing and processing text data.
Modules and packages: importing and using standard-library modules.

cards.title: What UTM tags are — and why humans get them wrong
cards.body:
**UTM parameters** are the little `?utm_source=...` labels at the end of a link. Google Analytics, HubSpot and every other analytics tool read them to answer one question: *which campaign brought this visitor?*

The problem: they are fragile. `Facebook`, `facebook` and `fb` show up as **three different sources** in your reports. A link that already has `?ref=nav` breaks if you blindly paste `?utm_source=...` on the end. A missing `#reviews` anchor sends people to the wrong part of the page.

Python's built-in `urllib.parse` module understands URL structure, so your script can:

1. **Split** a URL into parts (`urlparse`)
2. **Read** the existing query string into a dictionary (`parse_qsl`)
3. **Add/overwrite** the UTM keys (`dict.update`)
4. **Rebuild** the URL safely (`urlencode` + `urlunparse`), keeping the `#fragment` intact.
keyPoints: A URL has parts: scheme, domain, path, query (`?a=1&b=2`) and fragment (`#section`).
Never glue strings together to build URLs — use `urllib.parse` so existing parameters and anchors survive.
Normalise campaign names (lowercase, underscores, no symbols) so reports group correctly.
A dictionary's `.update()` adds new keys and overwrites existing ones — exactly what re-tagging needs.

realWorld.title: Why this matters in the real world
realWorld.body: A typical product launch needs 100+ tagged links across ads, emails, influencer posts and partner sites. Done by hand in a spreadsheet, that is around an hour and a half of copy-paste — and a single typo silently mis-attributes revenue for the whole quarter. This script turns it into a repeatable, zero-typo step you can hand to anyone on the team.

roi.note: Assumes ~120 links per campaign at ~45 s each, 4 campaigns per month.

cards.title: Walkthrough: tagging one link correctly

steps.explanation: Everything we need ships with Python — no installs. `urllib.parse` is the standard toolkit for taking URLs apart and putting them back together.
`urlparse` splits the link into named parts. Here `parts.path` is `/sale` and `parts.query` is `ref=nav`.
`parse_qsl` turns `ref=nav` into `[('ref', 'nav')]`, and `dict(...)` makes it `{'ref': 'nav'}` — easy to edit.
`.update()` adds the three UTM keys. If a key already existed (say an old `utm_source`), it is **overwritten** — so re-tagging a link is safe.
`urlencode` turns the dict back into `ref=nav&utm_source=...` (escaping spaces and symbols for you). `_replace` swaps in the new query, and `urlunparse` reassembles the full URL — fragment and all.
Notice the original `ref=nav` survived. Now try a URL ending in `#reviews` and press **Run** to see the anchor preserved.

challenge.title: Bulk-tag the Spring Sale links
challenge.prompt:
Your media team exported every Spring Sale link to `data/campaign_links.csv` (columns: `channel`, `url`). Finish the two functions so the script prints **one fully tagged URL per row**, in file order.

`CHANNEL_MAP` tells you the `utm_source` and `utm_medium` for each channel. The campaign name must be cleaned up with `slugify`.
requirements: `slugify(text)` returns lowercase text where runs of spaces/hyphens become a single `_` and any other symbol is removed ("Spring Sale 2026!" → "spring_sale_2026").
`add_utm(url, source, medium, campaign)` keeps existing query parameters (like `ref=nav`).
`add_utm` overwrites any existing `utm_*` values instead of duplicating them.
`add_utm` keeps the `#fragment` at the end of the URL.
Print only the tagged URLs — one per line.
challenge.starterCode:
import csv
import re
from urllib.parse import urlparse, urlunparse, parse_qsl, urlencode

CHANNEL_MAP = {
    "Facebook Ads": ("facebook", "paid_social"),
    "Newsletter": ("newsletter", "email"),
    "Google Ads": ("google", "cpc"),
    "Instagram Bio": ("instagram", "social"),
}
CAMPAIGN = "Spring Sale 2026!"


def slugify(text):
    # TODO: lowercase, collapse spaces/hyphens into "_", drop other symbols
    return text


def add_utm(url, source, medium, campaign):
    # TODO: keep existing params + #fragment, add/overwrite utm_* params
    return url


with open("data/campaign_links.csv", newline="") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):
        source, medium = CHANNEL_MAP[row["channel"]]
        print(add_utm(row["url"], source, medium, CAMPAIGN))

hints.text: For `slugify`, the `re` module is your friend: `re.sub(pattern, replacement, text)` replaces every match of `pattern`.
`r"[\s\-]+"` matches one or more spaces or hyphens. `r"[^a-z0-9_]"` matches anything that is *not* a lowercase letter, digit or underscore.
Re-use the walkthrough's `tag()` function for `add_utm` — just remember to call `slugify(campaign)`.

tests.name: slugify cleans campaign names
tests.failureHint: Lowercase first, then replace spaces with "_", then strip symbols like "!".

tests.name: slugify collapses messy spacing and hyphens
tests.failureHint: Strip the ends with `.strip()` and use `+` in your regex so several spaces/hyphens become one underscore.

tests.name: Existing query parameters are kept
The #fragment stays at the end
tests.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse

result = add_utm("https://x.com/boots#reviews", "google", "cpc", "x")
assert urlparse(result).fragment == "reviews"
assert result.endswith("#reviews")
tests.failureHint: Build the new URL from the parsed parts (`urlunparse`) instead of adding text to the end.

tests.name: Old utm_* values are overwritten, not duplicated
tests.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse, parse_qs

q = parse_qs(urlparse(add_utm("https://x.com/?utm_source=old&lang=en", "instagram", "social", "x")).query)
assert q["utm_source"] == ["instagram"]
assert q["lang"] == ["en"]

tests.name: add_utm slugifies the campaign itself
tests.code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse, parse_qs

q = parse_qs(urlparse(add_utm("https://x.com/", "a", "b", "Summer Launch - EU")).query)
assert q["utm_campaign"] == ["summer_launch_eu"]

tests.name: Prints all four tagged links in file order
tests.failureHint: Print exactly one URL per CSV row and nothing else.

questions.prompt: Your report shows traffic from `Facebook`, `facebook` and `FB` as three separate sources. What is the most robust fix?

options.text: Ask everyone to type more carefully
Generate links from a script with a fixed channel → source mapping
Delete the smaller sources from the report

questions.explanation: A single source of truth (`CHANNEL_MAP`) plus code that applies it guarantees identical labels every time.
`parse_qsl` returns a list of `(key, value)` pairs, and `dict()` turns those pairs into a dictionary.

questions.prompt: Complete the line that swaps the new query string into the parsed URL.
questions.explanation: `urlparse` returns a named tuple; `._replace(field=value)` returns a copy with one field changed.

questions.prompt: Why is `url + "?utm_source=fb"` a bad way to tag `https://shop.com/sale?ref=nav#top`?

options.text: It creates a second `?`, breaking the query string
The tag ends up after `#top`, so analytics never sees it

questions.explanation: String concatenation ignores URL structure: you get `...?ref=nav#top?utm_source=fb` — a broken query, and the tag is stuck inside the fragment, which browsers never send to the server.
